Hinged Dissection Of Vase

AreaGeometryCircles
Game: A vase is drawn with six equal curved sides, and we want to see whether its pieces can be rearranged into a square.
How to play: Drag the red dot or slide the bar to turn the pieces. Press the buttons to jump to the vase, halfway, or the square.
Look for the math

The border of this vase is six circular arcs of one radius R. The puzzle asks for its area, and the scroll bar turns three coloured pieces so that we can guess the answer before doing any arithmetic.

What the page claims

The cut-the-knot page says that adding four quarter-circle sectors to the top makes a square of side 2R, and so the vase has the same area as that square: 4R². The claim is true. The live page now embeds a GeoGebra picture in place of the Java applet; the original page, with the APPLET CODE="HingedDissectionOfVase" tag and two copies of the same slider, was checked in the Wayback Machine snapshot dated 5 April 2015.

Adding up the pieces

Ignore the two-pixel nudge the applet gives its neck arcs to hide seams. The bottom of the vase is a circle with its top quarter missing, so it has area 3πR²/4. Between the two radii up to O and the neck there is a triangle of area R²/2, then a rectangle √2R wide and √2R high. The two inward neck curves and the downward top curve each cut away a quarter-circle segment of area (π/4 − 1/2)R²:

3πR²/4 + R²/2 + [2R² − 3(π/4 − 1/2)R²] = 4R²

The π terms cancel exactly. The logic test checks this identity on every board size it tries and also counts the painted pixels on a fine grid.

Why the square appears

At 180 degrees the applet draws four lines through the circle's centre and the three upper points. They are the diagonals of a tilted square whose corners are (0, 0), (√2R, −√2R), (0, −2√2R) and (−√2R, −√2R). Each side is 2R, and the area is half the product of its diagonals: (2√2R)²/2 = 4R². The three quarters of the disk move to three corners, and the top of the vase fills the remaining gap: a genuine dissection, not a stretch.

Small quirks in the code

The applet reads a parameter called NSectors, but its drawing code never uses it; the picture always has three moving pieces. It also shifts the neck arcs down two pixels and gives the blue piece a half-pixel and one-degree correction. Those keep the drawing neat but play no part in the area, so the port keeps them in the picture and leaves them out of the formula.

Try this: press Square (180°), then Halfway (90°) and watch the same three coloured pieces travel back towards the vase.
